e.t: Agrippa is a personal name, referring to a person rather than describing an action, quality, or object. In the Greek New Testament, it appears eleven times, all in Acts, and is consistently rendered “Agrippa.” The name identifies the ruler who appears in the later part of Paul’s trial narrative. Since this word functions as a proper name, its meaning is chiefly its identification of that person; the surrounding passage supplies the details about his role and actions.

This word describes something done unwillingly—not by voluntary choice. It can characterize a person who acts without wanting to do so, or an action carried out without willingness. Its basic sense is therefore “not voluntary” or “unwilling.” In the Greek New Testament, it occurs once, in 1 Corinthians 9:17. The surrounding verse is needed to explain its particular force there; the word itself supplies the idea of unwillingness.

This word means “sin” or “sins,” referring to acts that violate God’s will. It points to wrongdoing as something that can be committed, forgiven, or held accountable before God. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs four times, including passages discussing forgiveness and the seriousness of sin. Its exact force in any particular verse is clarified by the surrounding context, but its central meaning remains an individual sinful act or acts.

This word means “rejected”: something refused, disapproved, or not accepted. It describes an object or matter viewed as unacceptable rather than approved. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs once, in 1 Timothy 4:4. Its basic sense is therefore clear, while the surrounding verse determines precisely what is being described as rejected. The word itself expresses exclusion from acceptance, not merely a difference of preference.

This word means a “deposit which guarantees” or “guarantee”—something given as assurance that what has been promised will be received. In the Greek New Testament, it describes a pledge connected with God’s promise, emphasizing certainty and assurance rather than a mere possibility. The word occurs three times, in 2 Corinthians and Ephesians, and each use concerns confidence in what God will ultimately provide.

Barak is a personal name referring to the biblical figure named in Hebrews 11:32. It functions as a name rather than a general word describing an action, quality, or object. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs once, in that single reference. The name identifies the person, while the surrounding verse and passage are needed to understand why he is mentioned there.

Blasphemy means “blasphemy,” referring to speech or expression that dishonors God or what is holy. It is a noun naming this kind of offense, and the plural form refers to multiple blasphemous expressions. In the Greek New Testament, the word occurs 18 times across 17 verses, showing that it is used as a distinct description for seriously dishonoring speech rather than for ordinary disagreement or criticism.

Gabbatha is a proper name, retained in English as “Gabbatha.” It identifies a named location rather than describing an action, quality, or relationship. This word appears once in the Greek New Testament, in John 19:13. Because the available meaning is the name itself and no verse text is provided here, its precise significance in that passage depends on the surrounding context. The word’s ordinary lexical function is therefore simply to designate Gabbatha.

e.t: This word means “ten,” the number that comes after nine and before eleven. It can also appear in the number “eighteen,” showing its use within a larger numbered expression. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs 26 times across 23 verses, commonly describing a count of people or things. Its basic function is numerical: it identifies quantity rather than expressing an action, quality, or relationship.

e.t: This word means “come” and can also express “now.” It is used to call someone to approach, arrive, or respond, often as a direct summons. The central idea is movement toward the speaker or a prompt for immediate action. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs nine times, so its normal sense remains focused and consistent rather than describing a broad range of ideas. Its exact force in a particular sentence depends on the surrounding words and passage.

This word means a decree: an official order or ruling issued by an authority. In the New Testament, it can describe an imperial command, official decisions given to believers, or regulations that function as binding requirements. The word appears five times in the Greek New Testament, with both singular and plural uses. Its central idea remains a formally stated rule or decision that carries authority, whether issued by a ruler or discussed as a regulation. The surrounding passage determines whose decree or regulation is in view.

This word describes what is possible or what someone is able to do—the presence or exercise of ability. It can refer to an action that can happen, a person who has the capacity to act, or something within reach. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs 32 times, showing regular use for ability and possibility rather than one narrow situation. Its exact force in a verse depends on what person or action it describes.

This word means “to live among,” describing the action of residing in the midst of other people. It presents presence within a community or surrounding group, rather than merely visiting or passing through. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs once, in 2 Peter 2:8. Its precise force in that verse depends on the surrounding passage, but its basic meaning is to make one’s home or remain among others.

This word refers to an abnormal or untimely birth. It is a noun describing a birth that occurs outside the expected time or manner. In the Greek New Testament, it appears only once, in 1 Corinthians 15:8. Without the surrounding verse text, its specific force in that passage cannot be explained here, but its basic meaning remains focused on an unusual birth or one occurring prematurely. The two closely related meanings, "abnormal birth" and "untimely birth," express the same central idea.

e.t: This word means “to command” or “to order,” describing an authoritative instruction given to someone. It presents the speaker as directing another person to do something, rather than merely making a suggestion. The word occurs 15 times in the Greek New Testament, across 15 verses, so it describes a recurring action of giving instructions in different settings. Its normal sense remains focused on issuing a command or order; the surrounding verse determines what specific instruction is being given. Matthew, Mark, and Hebrews are among the books where it appears.

This word means “place to live” or “residence,” referring to a dwelling or settled living place. It describes where someone lives rather than the person who lives there. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs only once, in Acts 1:20, so its precise force in that verse depends on the surrounding passage. Its basic sense remains a home, dwelling, or residence understood as a place of habitation.

e.t: This Greek New Testament verb means to remain, stay, or keep on rather than leave. It can describe continuing in a place or remaining in a situation, depending on the sentence. The word appears 16 times in the Greek New Testament, including uses rendered “stay” and “remain.” Its central idea is persistence: someone or something continues to be present instead of departing. The surrounding verse determines whether the emphasis is on physical location or continued action.

This word describes something helpful or useful—something that serves a good purpose or benefits others. It is used three times in the Greek New Testament, appearing in 2 Timothy and Philemon. In ordinary sentences, it points to practical value: a person, action, or thing that can be of service. The precise force in any particular verse depends on the surrounding passage, but its central idea is usefulness that genuinely helps.

“Trap” means a snare or means of catching and restraining someone. In the Greek New Testament, this word appears once, in Romans 11:9. Its basic sense points to something set before a person that can catch, entangle, or bring harm. The precise force of the word in Romans 11:9 must be understood from that verse and its surrounding passage, rather than from the word alone.

Iscariot is a personal name or designation, used to identify Judas in the Greek New Testament. It is not presented as a general quality, action, or spiritual condition, but as a distinctive name attached to a particular person. The word occurs 11 times in the Greek New Testament, across Matthew, Mark, Luke, and John. Its lexical gloss gives the name itself, while the surrounding passage identifies the specific role or significance associated with Judas in each occurrence.

e.t: This Greek New Testament word means “be fit,” “being fit,” or “to be fitting.” It describes something that is appropriate, suitable, or properly matching the situation. The word functions as an expression of what is fitting rather than naming a person, object, or event. It occurs twice in the Greek New Testament, so it is relatively uncommon there. Its exact force in either passage depends on the surrounding sentence and context.

This word means “wrongdoing,” describing conduct that is morally wrong or harmful. It functions as a participle, referring to someone who does wrong rather than merely experiencing a bad situation. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs three times, all in 1 Peter. Its basic sense is broad enough to cover wrongful behavior without specifying one particular offense. The surrounding verse determines what kind of wrongdoing is being discussed, but the word itself points to the person’s blameworthy action.

This Greek New Testament word refers to the inside of the body, especially the belly, stomach, or womb. It can describe the bodily place where food is received or where a child is carried, so its precise English rendering depends on the setting. The glosses include “any and all internal organs,” “belly,” “stomach,” and “womb.” It occurs 22 times in the Greek New Testament, covering both ordinary bodily references and references to the womb. Its central idea is the body’s inner region or organs.

This word describes something futile or worthless—something that lacks useful result, lasting value, or real effectiveness. It can describe human thinking, speech, religious practice, or a way of life when these fail to achieve what they appear intended to accomplish. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs six times across six verses. Its basic sense is negative: it points to emptiness, uselessness, or lack of benefit rather than merely something small or unimportant. The surrounding verse determines exactly what is being judged as futile or worthless.

This word means “midair,” referring to the open space above the ground. It describes a location rather than an object, person, or action. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs three times, all in Revelation: 8:13, 14:6, and 19:17. Its basic meaning remains focused and concrete—the area suspended between the earth and the sky. The surrounding verse determines what is present or happening in that space, but the word itself identifies the location as midair.

e.t: This word means “to suppose”—to form an assumption or consider something to be so. It describes an act of thought rather than direct knowledge or certainty. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs three times, showing a focused use for expressing what someone believes, assumes, or reckons to be true. The surrounding verse determines whether that supposition is accurate, mistaken, or presented for consideration. Its basic sense remains the mental act of assuming something.

The word means “paradise,” naming a distinct place or realm. In the Greek New Testament, it appears three times, in Luke, 2 Corinthians, and Revelation. Each occurrence carries the same central meaning rather than presenting several unrelated senses. The word therefore identifies paradise as a specific destination or sphere mentioned in biblical hope. Its precise emphasis in each passage depends on the surrounding verse and passage.

e.t: This word means “mourning” or “to mourn”: to express deep sorrow, especially over loss, separation, or serious wrongdoing. It describes the outward or inward response of a grieving person rather than ordinary sadness. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs 10 times, showing its use for personal grief, sorrow connected with loss, and sorrow over sinful conduct. Its precise force in any verse depends on the surrounding passage, but the central idea remains genuine grief that calls for expression or recognition.

e.t: “To earn more” means to gain additional profit or increase what one already has. This Greek New Testament verb describes an action rather than a person or object: someone works with what is entrusted to him so that it produces a greater return. It occurs once in the Greek New Testament, in Luke 19:16. The word itself states the increase being sought; the surrounding passage is needed to explain the specific situation and application.

This word refers to grain, especially wheat, the edible crop produced by a field and gathered at harvest. It is a noun used for the plant or its grain, and its meaning remains concrete rather than describing an abstract quality. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs 14 times in 14 verses. Its repeated use in farming and harvest language makes it a straightforward agricultural term, whether the surrounding passage speaks of sowing, growing, separating, or gathering. The normal sense is simply grain or wheat.

This word refers to a leafy branch or branch covered with leaves. It is a concrete term for vegetation rather than an abstract idea or action. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs once, in Mark 11:8, so its normal meaning is represented by that single use. The surrounding verse and passage are needed to explain its particular role there; the word itself identifies the leafy branch being mentioned.

e.t: This Greek New Testament word means “to assemble” or “to gather together.” It describes bringing people or things together into one place or group, whether the gathering is intentional or simply the result of people coming together. It occurs 59 times in the Greek New Testament, so it is a recurring word for collective gathering rather than a rare or specialized action. Its precise force in any verse depends on what is being gathered and the surrounding sentence.

This word means “bodily,” describing something connected with the physical body rather than the inner or spiritual life. It functions as a descriptive word, clarifying that an action, practice, or condition concerns the body. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs twice, in Luke 3:22 and 1 Timothy 4:8. The surrounding verse determines precisely what bodily matter is being described, but the central meaning remains physical or body-related.

This word means “wonder” or “wonders,” referring to remarkable acts or events that inspire amazement. It describes something extraordinary and striking, especially when people recognize that what they see is beyond the ordinary. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs 16 times and is consistently rendered “wonders.” The word appears in passages discussing signs and remarkable works, but its precise force in any particular verse depends on the surrounding context.

This word means “third”. It identifies something as occupying the third place in a sequence, or as happening for the third time. In the New Testament, it is used 56 times, including references to a third day, a third occasion, or a third person or group in an order. Its central idea is position or repetition counted after the first and second. The related phrase “for the third time” makes the repeated-event sense explicit. The word appears from Matthew through Revelation and consistently expresses this numerical order.

This word means “Pharisee” or “Pharisees,” referring to the people identified by that name in the Greek New Testament. It is a group designation rather than a description of an action or quality. The word appears 98 times in 93 New Testament verses, with especially frequent use in Matthew, Luke, and John. Its precise significance in any particular passage depends on the surrounding verse and discussion.

This word means “news,” referring to a report or message that has become known. It is a noun describing information communicated from one person or place to others, rather than an action or personal quality. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs twice, showing that it is a specific term for a report that spreads or is heard. Its precise force in either passage depends on the surrounding verse and context.

This word means “murderer,” referring to a person who has killed another. It can also appear as “murderers” when describing more than one person. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs seven times across seven verses, consistently identifying people by this serious act rather than describing a general attitude or minor wrongdoing. Its precise force in any particular verse depends on the surrounding passage.
